prov_cuu_cao.name: Cửu Cao
prov_cuu_cao.lore: Reed marsh and wet woodland along a slow river, with a little steppe and one bare spur of mountain at the edge. Its people cut reed, net marsh fish and keep the roosts of Cửu Cao Phái, whose cranes are the only sky traffic here. Since 874 the crane riders have also held the holdings the Pivot took from Phá Quân Môn, and the marsh villages pay their dues in reed and fish to the sect rather than to the Pivot's clerks.

prov_p111.name: Ba Quang
prov_p111.lore: A strip of forest coast and small stepped lakes below the ridges. Its people fish the lakes and the shore and ferry Cửu Cao's riders over the water. The ruins of an older port lie on the coast to the east, a reminder of why Ba Quang builds well back from the tide line.

prov_p112.name: Hạc Quy
prov_p112.lore: Gentle forested river country with marsh meadows where the cranes come down each year. Villagers farm millet and beans and keep the landing pool clear for the birds. A small Wood vein lies in the woods west of the village, and the crane riders rest their mounts on it after long flights.

prov_p113.name: Lộc Uyển
prov_p113.lore: High meadows and open forest where the steppe begins, under Thiên Xu's old ban on hunting. Its people keep goats, gather shed antlers and cut hay. On a wooded rise stand the empty halls of Bạch Lộc Quán, the little abbey that first asked the Pivot to protect the deer.

prov_p34.name: Khai Dương
prov_p34.lore: The forest country around the port of Khai Dương Thành, cut by a river that reaches the sea under the city walls. Farms and timber lots feed the city, and its quays ship timber, furs and Dao Quang iron along the northern coast. The woods inland are kept for the city's shipwrights and its morning fires.

prov_p64.name: Bích Khê
prov_p64.lore: Forested hills around the green brook of Bích Khê Trấn, with a few steppe clearings on the high ground. Jade-pickers and carvers live by the brook, woodcutters by the hills. Downstream the brook runs through a stand of firs that the town forbids anyone to fell.

prov_p65.name: Thanh Bách
prov_p65.lore: Rolling forest and steppe on the northern road around Thanh Bách Thành. Its farms grow wheat and millet on the clearings, and ore carts from the southern mountains roll through it to the coast. The old cypress wood north of the city gives the city its name and its coffins.

prov_r6_1.name: Hải Tùng
prov_r6_1.lore: Low forest coast of pines that grow right down to the shingle. A few fishing families and resin tappers live here, and their boats sell catch and pitch at Khai Dương. Inland the pines grow so close that the coast road has never been cut through them.

prov_r6_10.name: Cao Mục
prov_r6_10.lore: Forest on the lower slopes, open steppe above and a knot of bare mountain to the west. Shepherds drive their flocks up to the summer grass and down to the woods for winter. They say the high ground here was found warm under the snow by the first shepherds of Dao Quang.

prov_r6_11.name: Lâm Biên
prov_r6_11.lore: A wide, dark forest of the inner ridges with no river, crossed by timber tracks. Woodcutters live at its edges and seldom go deep, for the boars of the high woods are big and short-tempered. In the middle stand the burned walls of Chi Hương Trấn, the resin town lost to fire.

prov_r6_12.name: Nhân Sâm
prov_r6_12.lore: Broad forest of the ridge country, rising to fir woods on the higher ground. Its people dig wild ginseng and other roots under the trees and sell them to Thiên Xu's alchemists at Khai Dương. Root diggers keep their patches secret even from their own children until they are too old to climb.

prov_r6_13.name: Hữu Bật Lĩnh
prov_r6_13.gloss: Ridge of the Right Assistant Star
prov_r6_13.lore: Steep mountains with a strip of forest along a river, empty but for hunters and patrols. It is named for the hidden star said to stand beside the Dipper, as Phụ Tinh stands on the other side. Herb hunters climb its cold ridges for mountain flowers, and the Pivot's patrols pass through on the way to Tinh Tủy Mạch.

prov_r6_14.name: Sương Kích Lĩnh
prov_r6_14.lore: High ice-capped mountains dropping straight into the northern sea, with no farmland and no village. It takes its name from the rusted iron stakes on Phụ Tinh Phong, where Phá Quân Môn drilled at night, which the frost coats white every winter. Only Thiên Xu's patrols and a few bold herb hunters come here.

prov_r6_15.name: Phóng Mã
prov_r6_15.lore: Forested hills with open steppe glades where horses are turned out to graze. Its people breed sturdy forest horses for Thiên Xu's couriers and the northern road. Wolf packs hunt the wooded ridges east of the pastures, and the herders ride in pairs.

prov_r6_16.name: Mặc Yên
prov_r6_16.lore: Rough upland of forest, steppe and red badland gullies at the southern edge of the forests. Its people burn pine in closed kilns for soot and press it into the ink sticks Thiên Xu's clerks write with. Great bears live in the high woods, and the ink-makers leave a cake of honey at the forest edge each autumn.

prov_r6_17.name: Lý Ngư
prov_r6_17.lore: Forest and mountain flank along a river that comes down from the high ranges. Villagers fish the river for carp and float timber down it. A vein of Wood and Metal qi in the woods above the village draws the Pivot's ironworkers, who come to temper tools there.

prov_r6_18.name: Lộc Tồn Lĩnh
prov_r6_18.gloss: Ridge of the Lộc Tồn Star
prov_r6_18.lore: Forested mountains along a river, named for the third of the Dipper's star-lords in Thiên Xu's reckoning. No village stands here; miners come up the river to the red iron diggings and go down again before the snow. Its red-crested peak is a landmark for crane riders.

prov_r6_19.name: Trường Canh Lĩnh
prov_r6_19.lore: Bare high mountains of black rock below Trích Tinh Phong, where the evening star is first seen over the ridge. Nothing grows here but lichen, and no one lives here but the guard of Tinh Tủy Mạch. The guard has stood since 470 and was doubled in 1188; its fires are the only lights on the ridge at night.

prov_r6_2.name: Mộc Phiệt
prov_r6_2.lore: Deep river forest in the west of the ridge country. Its people fell timber and float it down the river to the coast in great rafts each spring. Walnut groves on the drier ground give them a second harvest in the autumn.

prov_r6_20.name: Chiên Mao
prov_r6_20.lore: Open steppe and thin forest above red badlands on the southern edge of Dao Quang. Herders keep sheep and goats and beat their wool into felt for tents and boots. An Earth vein lies under the steppe nearby, and its warm ground keeps the grass green into winter.

prov_r6_21.name: Liêm Trinh Nguyên
prov_r6_21.gloss: Plain of the Liêm Trinh Star
prov_r6_21.lore: Broken country of steppe, mountain, forest and badland named for the fifth of the Dipper's star-lords. Nobody farms it; herders pass through in summer, and prospectors come for the Metal vein hidden in its woods. The land is dry and the springs are few and far apart.

prov_r6_22.name: Vũ Khúc Lĩnh
prov_r6_22.gloss: Ridge of the Vũ Khúc Star
prov_r6_22.lore: High forested mountains named for the Dipper's warrior star. In Phá Quân Môn's day its forts watched the southern roads, and their walls still stand on the heights. Today only woodcutters and patrols climb it, and they do not camp in the old forts.

prov_r6_23.name: Tham Lang Lĩnh
prov_r6_23.gloss: Ridge of the Tham Lang Star
prov_r6_23.lore: Steep mountains and forest on the eastern side of the ranges, named for the first of the Dipper's star-lords. Lead and silver are dug here by a few hard crews. In 871 Thiên Xu camped here to besiege Phá Quân Môn, and the siege lines can still be traced on the slopes.

prov_r6_24.name: Văn Khúc Lĩnh
prov_r6_24.gloss: Ridge of the Văn Khúc Star
prov_r6_24.lore: Tall bare mountains named for the Dipper's star of letters. Tin is dug on its lower slopes and carried down to the coast. Scholars of the Pivot climb its brush-shaped peak to compose poems, and most of the poems are about how cold it is.

prov_r6_25.name: Thiên Thê Lĩnh
prov_r6_25.lore: The high spine of Dao Quang, crowned by Trích Tinh Phong and its thousand rock-cut steps. Pilgrims climb the stair all summer; no one lives here but the keepers of a few rest huts. On a shoulder below the summit lie the broken gate and walls of Phá Quân Môn.

prov_r6_26.name: Hàn Đẩu Lĩnh
prov_r6_26.lore: A wall of glaciered peaks east of Trích Tinh Phong, part of the same massif. Jade is cut from the rock high on its flanks, in a short summer season. Herders say the Dipper hangs lowest over these peaks in winter, as if it had come down to rest.

prov_r6_27.name: Hồng Thạch Câu
prov_r6_27.lore: Red badland gullies and bare mountain south of the forests. Copper is dug from the red rock, and the copper crews are the only people here. Rain is rare, and when it comes the gullies run red with mud for a day.

prov_r6_28.name: Bằng Dực Lĩnh
prov_r6_28.lore: High mountain and badland under the cliffs of Bằng Sào Nhai, where a roc nests. No one lives here, and herders keep their flocks well away. Lodestone is dug on the ridge by crews who work under rock overhangs, out of sight of the sky.

prov_r6_29.name: Hoang Đài Nguyên
prov_r6_29.lore: Stepped badland terraces and low mountain at the southern edge of Dao Quang. The ground is too dry to farm, and only herders cross it in spring when the grass comes. Its stone drum peak is said to boom when storms come off the heartland.

prov_r6_3.name: Huyền Chi
prov_r6_3.lore: Damp forest along a river, thick with old logs and fungus. Its people gather wood-ear and dark lingzhi and dry them on racks for the markets of Khai Dương. The pine woods on the high ground are tapped for resin by the same families.

prov_r6_30.name: Mặc Thạch Lĩnh
prov_r6_30.lore: Dark mountains and forest whose black slate splits into fine inkstones. A small quarry crew cuts the slate and sends it to Thiên Xu's clerks and scholars. No farms stand here; the crews eat what comes up the mule path.

prov_r6_31.name: Hàn Mạch
prov_r6_31.lore: High mixed country of forest, steppe and red badland in the south-east of Dao Quang. Its people grow buckwheat on the cold upland where wheat will not ripen, and keep goats on the rest. Stone lizards bask on the badland ledges, and children are taught not to climb there.

prov_r6_32.name: Thiết Lăng Câu
prov_r6_32.lore: Sharp-edged badland ridges and mountain at the southern edge of the region. No one lives here, but turquoise is dug from the copper-stained rock and carried north. The gullies are bitter cold at night and hot by noon.

prov_r6_33.name: Liệt Thạch Câu
prov_r6_33.lore: Mountain and badland where frost has split the rock into fields of broken blocks. It is empty of people and nearly empty of water. Travellers crossing to the heartland follow the cairns and do not leave them.

prov_r6_34.name: Ẩn Lộc Lĩnh
prov_r6_34.lore: Forested mountain with high grassy clearings on the southern ranges. Deer that leave the park at Lộc Uyển are said to come here to die, and hunters will not shoot in its woods. Herb gatherers come up in summer and sleep in bark huts.

prov_r6_4.name: Hải Đê
prov_r6_4.lore: Low forest coast, part of it lying below the level of the sea behind an old earth dike. Its people farm and fish behind the dike and keep it in repair together each autumn. Inland, the wind off the sea has bent the pines flat to the ground.

prov_r6_5.name: Tạo Chu
prov_r6_5.lore: Forest coast west of Khai Dương, where the firs grow tall and straight down to a sheltered bay. Its people build boats and ships of fir and sell them along the northern coast. The yards work for Khai Dương's merchants, and every keel is laid facing the dawn.

prov_r6_6.name: Mật Phong
prov_r6_6.lore: Wide forested hills in the west of Dao Quang, with no great river. Its people keep bees in log hives and sell honey and wax as far as Thạch Kiều Thành. A Wood vein lies in the hills, and the bees that forage near it make a honey prized by alchemists.

prov_r6_7.name: Tích Thán
prov_r6_7.lore: Forested hills between the western woods and the coast, smoky with charcoal kilns. Its people burn oak and poplar into charcoal for the smiths of Khai Dương and Thanh Bách. They cut in a ring and let each part of the forest grow back for twenty years.

prov_r6_8.name: Cự Môn
prov_r6_8.lore: Forest coast backed by the first steep mountains of the east, named for the second of the Dipper's star-lords. Its town ships timber and ore and serves the patrols bound for the high ranges. Above the town stand the empty streets of Hắc Thạch Trấn, a mining town of Phá Quân Môn that was never resettled.

prov_r6_9.name: Kình Bối Nhai
prov_r6_9.lore: Steep mountains that rise straight out of the northern sea in long humped cliffs. There is no anchorage and no farmland, only seabirds and wind. Fishermen of Cự Môn read the weather by the cloud on its tide-watching peak.

prov_cuu_cao_forest_1.name: Hạc Tê Lâm
prov_cuu_cao_forest_1.look: Tall pines on a low rise above the marsh, their crowns flattened and white with droppings where cranes stand at dusk.
prov_cuu_cao_forest_1.lore: Young cranes of Cửu Cao Phái roost here before they are trusted on the towers. The riders forbid felling any tree a crane has stood on.

prov_p111_beast_lair_1.name: Kiêu Minh Lâm
prov_p111_beast_lair_1.look: A dim stand of old oaks between the lakes, hung with owl pellets and silent by day.
prov_p111_beast_lair_1.lore: Spirit owls with wings as wide as a boat hunt here at night and take lambs and dogs. Ba Quang's fishermen will not row past it after dark.

prov_p111_ruin_2.name: Cựu Tân Trấn
prov_p111_ruin_2.look: Stone footings and a broken quay on the shore, half buried in sand and shingle, with sea grass growing in the old streets.
prov_p111_ruin_2.lore: A small port that ferried goods along the coast from 420. In 968 a storm tide drove over the quay and took half the town; the rest moved inland to the lakes of Ba Quang.

prov_p112_spirit_vein_1.name: Hạc Tức Mạch
prov_p112_spirit_vein_1.look: A hollow in the woods where the pines grow twice as thick as their neighbours and the moss is bright green even in winter.
prov_p112_spirit_vein_1.lore: A small vein (linh mạch) whose qi (linh khí) runs to Wood. Cửu Cao's riders rest tired cranes here, and the birds sleep a whole day after.

prov_p113_forest_1.name: Lão Du Lâm
prov_p113_forest_1.look: A line of old elms along the edge of the steppe, bent away from the wind, with deer trails worn through the grass beneath.
prov_p113_forest_1.lore: The elms shelter Lộc Uyển's deer from the steppe wind in early spring. Villagers gather the elm seed in famine years and grind it into cakes.

prov_p113_ruin_2.name: Bạch Lộc Quán
prov_p113_ruin_2.look: Low moss-grown halls on a wooded rise, their roofs fallen in, with a stone deer standing headless in the court.
prov_p113_ruin_2.lore: Hermits who fed the wild deer founded this small abbey in 370 and asked the Pivot to ban hunting in the meadow, which it did in 380. Its last master died in 612 without a disciple, and the halls were left to the deer.

prov_p34_forest_1.name: Thần Hi Lâm
prov_p34_forest_1.look: An oak and beech forest on the east side of Khai Dương, so open that the first light runs far under its trees.
prov_p34_forest_1.lore: Khai Dương's bakers gather their kindling here before dawn. The city keeps it as a common wood, and no one may fence it.

prov_p64_forest_1.name: Khê Sam Lâm
prov_p64_forest_1.look: Straight red-barked firs stand in the shallows of the green brook, their roots knotted like knees above the water.
prov_p64_forest_1.lore: Bích Khê Trấn forbids felling these firs, since their roots hold the brook bed where the jade pebbles lie. Carvers say the best stones are found where the knees are thickest.

prov_p65_forest_1.name: Cổ Bách Lâm
prov_p65_forest_1.look: A dark wood of ancient cypresses north of Thanh Bách Thành, their trunks twisted and grey and their scent heavy in the air.
prov_p65_forest_1.lore: Thanh Bách cuts its coffin wood here, one tree for each official who dies in office. The oldest trees are tied with red cord and may never be cut.

prov_r6_1_village_1.name: Hải Tùng Thôn
prov_r6_1_village_1.look: A handful of tarred timber houses on the shingle under leaning pines, with resin pots smoking by the boats.
prov_r6_1_village_1.lore: Its families fish the coast and tap the pines for pitch, which they sell to the boatyards. Every boat here is caulked with pitch from the family's own trees.

prov_r6_1_forest_2.name: Mật Tùng Lâm
prov_r6_1_forest_2.look: A dense forest of black-barked pines, so close-grown that it is dusk under them at noon.
prov_r6_1_forest_2.lore: The coast road has never been cut through it, and travellers go round by the shore. Resin tappers work only its edges and say the middle is full of fallen trunks no one has ever cleared.

prov_r6_10_village_1.name: Cao Mục Thôn
prov_r6_10_village_1.look: Stone sheepfolds and low turf-roofed houses on an open steppe shoulder, with flocks spread over the slope below.
prov_r6_10_village_1.lore: Its shepherds drive their sheep to the high grass each summer and down into the woods for winter. Wool and cheese go down to Bích Khê on market days.

prov_r6_10_peak_2.name: Tức Ngưu Sơn
prov_r6_10_peak_2.look: A broad round-backed mountain of grey rock above the forest, shaped like an ox lying down to rest.
prov_r6_10_peak_2.lore: Its qi runs to Earth, slow and steady, and shepherds say flocks grazed on its flanks never stray. Cultivators of Earth arts sit on its back to settle their foundations.

prov_r6_11_village_1.name: Lâm Biên Thôn
prov_r6_11_village_1.look: Log houses where the timber tracks leave the forest, with stacked trunks and sawpits along the lane.
prov_r6_11_village_1.lore: Woodcutters live here and work the edge of the deep forest. They go into the high woods only in groups, with dogs, because of the boars.

prov_r6_11_beast_lair_2.name: Sơn Trư Cương
prov_r6_11_beast_lair_2.look: A wooded ridge rooted bare in great furrows, with trees scarred waist-high by tusks.
prov_r6_11_beast_lair_2.lore: Spirit boars as big as oxen live here and dig up the forest floor for roots. Their bristles make fine brushes, and hunters who take them seldom try twice.

prov_r6_11_ruin_3.name: Chi Hương Trấn
prov_r6_11_ruin_3.look: Blackened stone walls and the stumps of a gate tower in a clearing of young pines, with charred beams still lying in the lanes.
prov_r6_11_ruin_3.lore: A resin town that boiled pitch for the coast from 330. In the dry summer of 712 a fire began in its pitch yards and burned the town and the forest around it; no one rebuilt.

prov_r6_12_village_1.name: Nhân Sâm Thôn
prov_r6_12_village_1.look: A forest village of bark-roofed houses with racks of drying roots under every eave.
prov_r6_12_village_1.lore: Its people dig wild ginseng and sell it to Thiên Xu's alchemists at Khai Dương. A digger's patch passes only from parent to child, shown once, on the parent's last climb.

prov_r6_12_forest_2.name: Cung Sam Lâm
prov_r6_12_forest_2.look: Tall dark firs on the high ridge, often wrapped in cloud, their trunks bearded with grey lichen.
prov_r6_12_forest_2.lore: The fir here is light and springy, and the Pivot's bowyers and formation masters buy it for bows and frames. Cloud sits in the forest most mornings until noon.

prov_r6_13_peak_1.name: Ẩn Tinh Phong
prov_r6_13_peak_1.look: A narrow grey peak above the river forest, whose summit is lost in cloud on most nights.
prov_r6_13_peak_1.lore: It is named for the hidden assistant star of the Dipper, which star-readers say can only be seen from here on one night a year. Its qi runs to Metal, sharp and cold.

prov_r6_15_village_1.name: Phóng Mã Thôn
prov_r6_15_village_1.look: Timber stables and paddock fences on a steppe glade ringed by forest, with herds grazing loose beyond.
prov_r6_15_village_1.lore: Its people breed sturdy forest horses for Thiên Xu's couriers on the northern road. The herds are turned out loose in summer and rounded up by riders working in pairs.

prov_r6_15_beast_lair_2.name: Quần Lang Cương
prov_r6_15_beast_lair_2.look: A wooded ridge of broken rock with dens under every boulder and old bones scattered in the leaves.
prov_r6_15_beast_lair_2.lore: Grey spirit wolves den here in packs of twenty or more and hunt the horse herds in winter. Phóng Mã's riders burn torches along the pasture edge on the longest nights.

prov_r6_16_village_1.name: Mặc Yên Thôn
prov_r6_16_village_1.look: Soot-black houses around long brick kilns that smoulder day and night, with ink cakes drying on boards in the sun.
prov_r6_16_village_1.lore: Its people burn pine in closed kilns, gather the soot and press it into ink sticks for Thiên Xu's clerks. The best sticks are scented with musk and stamped with the Dipper.

prov_r6_16_beast_lair_2.name: Đại Hùng Lâm
prov_r6_16_beast_lair_2.look: Old forest high on the ridge, with trunks clawed bare and beehives torn open in the branches.
prov_r6_16_beast_lair_2.lore: Great spirit bears live here, named by the villagers for the stars of the Dipper, which they call the Great Bear. Each autumn the ink-makers leave a cake of honey at the forest edge, and the bears have not come down in living memory.

prov_r6_17_village_1.name: Lý Ngư Thôn
prov_r6_17_village_1.look: A river village of grey roofs with fish traps of woven willow set in the shallows and log rafts tied along the bank.
prov_r6_17_village_1.lore: Its people trap carp and guide timber rafts down the river. A carp that leaps the weir in spring is let go, for luck.

prov_r6_17_spirit_vein_2.name: Thiết Mộc Mạch
prov_r6_17_spirit_vein_2.look: A wooded slope where the trees grow slow and black, their wood so hard that axes ring off it.
prov_r6_17_spirit_vein_2.lore: A vein whose qi runs to Wood and Metal together. Thiên Xu's ironworkers bring their tools here to be tempered, and the ironwood is cut only for array frames.

prov_r6_18_peak_1.name: Xích Quan Phong
prov_r6_18_peak_1.look: A ridge-top of jagged red-grey rock teeth standing above the forest like a rooster's comb.
prov_r6_18_peak_1.lore: Crane riders steer by it on the way to Tinh Tủy Mạch. Its qi runs to Metal.

prov_r6_18_mine_2.name: Giả Thiết Khoáng
prov_r6_18_mine_2.look: Rust-red pits in the mountainside above the river, with ore heaps and a log slide down to the water.
prov_r6_18_mine_2.lore: Crews dig red iron ore here in summer and slide it to the river for rafting to Cự Môn. They leave before the snow and never winter on the ridge.

prov_r6_2_village_1.name: Mộc Phiệt Thôn
prov_r6_2_village_1.look: Long timber sheds and log booms on a river bend, with great rafts being lashed together on the bank.
prov_r6_2_village_1.lore: Each spring its people float the winter's timber down to the coast on huge rafts and walk home along the bank. A raftsman who loses his raft walks home without speaking.

prov_r6_2_forest_2.name: Hồ Đào Lâm
prov_r6_2_forest_2.look: Broad walnut trees on the drier hills, their ground thick with husks in autumn.
prov_r6_2_forest_2.lore: The walnut harvest is Mộc Phiệt's second crop. The trees are counted and owned by families, and some have been owned by the same family since before the Pivot came.

prov_r6_20_village_1.name: Chiên Mao Thôn
prov_r6_20_village_1.look: Round felt-roofed houses on the open steppe, with wool spread on mats and women beating it with sticks.
prov_r6_20_village_1.lore: Its herders make felt for tents, boots and saddle cloths and sell it down the northern road. Felt from here is said to keep out rain for ten years.

prov_r6_20_spirit_vein_2.name: Noãn Thổ Mạch
prov_r6_20_spirit_vein_2.look: A low swell of steppe where the grass stays green through winter and frost never lies on the ground.
prov_r6_20_spirit_vein_2.lore: Its qi runs to Earth, warm and deep, like the ground the first shepherds of Dao Quang found. Herders bring their flocks here in the hardest winters, and the Pivot lets them.

prov_r6_21_spirit_vein_1.name: Tàng Kim Mạch
prov_r6_21_spirit_vein_1.look: A forested hollow among bare hills where thin gold seams glint in a rock face under the roots.
prov_r6_21_spirit_vein_1.lore: A vein whose qi runs to Metal, found by a prospector who could not dig the gold out. The gold, the Pivot's assayers say, is the qi itself made visible, and will not come away.

prov_r6_22_peak_1.name: Xích Sam Phong
prov_r6_22_peak_1.look: A forested peak whose red-barked firs grow almost to the summit rock.
prov_r6_22_peak_1.lore: Its qi runs to Wood, unusual so high in the ranges. Woodcutters who climb it to cut firs leave the topmost tree standing.

prov_r6_22_ruin_2.name: Vọng Tinh Bảo
prov_r6_22_ruin_2.look: A square stone fort on a forested height, its gate burned and its walls still standing to the parapet.
prov_r6_22_ruin_2.lore: Phá Quân Môn built it in 742 to watch the southern roads. When the rebellion was crushed in 874 its garrison surrendered without a fight, and the fort was burned and left.

prov_r6_23_peak_1.name: Khiếu Lang Phong
prov_r6_23_peak_1.look: A sharp white-grey fang of rock above the eastern forests, where the wind howls in the cracks.
prov_r6_23_peak_1.lore: Its qi runs to Metal, keen and restless. Sword cultivators climb it to sharpen their intent.

prov_r6_23_mine_2.name: Duyên Ngân Khoáng
prov_r6_23_mine_2.look: Grey spoil heaps below a few adits, with a small smelting hearth and a heap of lead pigs by the path.
prov_r6_23_mine_2.lore: Lead and a little silver are dug here and smelted on the spot. The crews are paid in Thiên Xu's silver coin, which they like to say they dug themselves.

prov_r6_23_ruin_3.name: Vi Thành Trại
prov_r6_23_ruin_3.look: Earth banks and rotted palisade stakes in a ring on a mountain shoulder, with fire pits still black inside.
prov_r6_23_ruin_3.lore: Thiên Xu raised this camp in 871 to besiege Phá Quân Môn and abandoned it when the rebel gate fell in 874. Soldiers' names scratched on its stones can still be read.

prov_r6_24_peak_1.name: Chấp Bút Phong
prov_r6_24_peak_1.look: A slender rock summit standing upright above the ridge like a brush held to paper.
prov_r6_24_peak_1.lore: Scholars of the Pivot climb it to write poems on the summit. Its qi runs to Metal.

prov_r6_24_mine_2.name: Bạch Tích Khoáng
prov_r6_24_mine_2.look: A few small adits on a low mountain slope, with ore washed in a cold stream and spread to dry on flat stones.
prov_r6_24_mine_2.lore: Tin from here is carried to Khai Dương and alloyed into bronze for the Pivot's bells and mirrors.

prov_r6_26_peak_1.name: Thị Tinh Phong
prov_r6_26_peak_1.look: A great white glacier peak standing just east of Trích Tinh Phong, a little lower, like an attendant beside a throne.
prov_r6_26_peak_1.lore: Pilgrims call it Trích Tinh's servant. Its qi runs to Metal and Water, cold as its ice.

prov_r6_26_mine_2.name: Tuyết Ngọc Khoáng
prov_r6_26_mine_2.look: A small cut high on a bare slope near the ice, with blocks of pale stone roped on sledges.
prov_r6_26_mine_2.lore: White jade is cut here in a short summer season and sledged down over the snow. The Pivot's seal-cutters take the best of it.

prov_r6_27_peak_1.name: Chu Bình Phong
prov_r6_27_peak_1.look: A long flat-faced red cliff peak above the badland gullies, glowing at sunset.
prov_r6_27_peak_1.lore: Its qi runs to Earth with a warmth of Fire. Copper crews read the time of day by the colour of its face.

prov_r6_27_mine_2.name: Hồng Câu Khoáng
prov_r6_27_mine_2.look: Green-stained pits in red rock, with a line of water jars carried up from far below.
prov_r6_27_mine_2.lore: Copper is dug here and carried north by mule. Water is so short that the crews bring every drink up the gully.

prov_r6_28_mine_1.name: Chỉ Nam Khoáng
prov_r6_28_mine_1.look: A dark adit under a rock overhang, its mouth bristling with iron nails that have flown to the stone and stuck.
prov_r6_28_mine_1.lore: Lodestone from here goes to the Pivot's formation masters and to compass makers. The crews work under the overhang, out of sight of the roc.

prov_r6_29_peak_1.name: Thạch Cổ Phong
prov_r6_29_peak_1.look: A round, drum-shaped knob of rock on the badland terraces, hollow at its base.
prov_r6_29_peak_1.lore: Wind in its hollow booms before storms, and herders drive their flocks to shelter when it sounds. Its qi runs to Earth.

prov_r6_3_village_1.name: Huyền Chi Thôn
prov_r6_3_village_1.look: Damp bark-roofed houses in the forest with mushroom logs stacked under the trees and drying racks along the lanes.
prov_r6_3_village_1.lore: Its people grow and gather wood-ear and dark lingzhi and sell them dried at Khai Dương. They tap the pines above the village for resin in the dry months.

prov_r6_3_forest_2.name: Chu Tùng Lâm
prov_r6_3_forest_2.look: Tall red-trunked pines on the high ground above the river, their bark peeling in papery strips.
prov_r6_3_forest_2.lore: The pine nuts and resin feed Huyền Chi through the winter. Talisman (phù lục) makers buy the resin to fix their ink.

prov_r6_3_minor_seat_p.name: Họa Tinh Đường
prov_r6_3_minor_seat_p.look: A low hall of dark timber in a forest clearing, its walls hung with long paper strips painted with the Dipper and drying in the wind.
prov_r6_3_minor_seat_p.lore: Talisman makers who paint the stars of the Dipper onto paper founded this hall in 910 and swore to Thiên Xu. They grind their ink from Mặc Yên soot and fix it with pine resin, and a talisman from here will not run in the rain.

sect.name: Họa Tinh Đường
sect.craft: talismans (phù lục) painted with the Dipper

prov_r6_30_peak_1.name: Huyền Vũ Phong
prov_r6_30_peak_1.look: A dark, heavy peak of black slate above the forests, shaped like a tortoise's shell.
prov_r6_30_peak_1.lore: It is named for the northern constellation of the Black Warrior. Its qi runs to Water and Metal.

prov_r6_30_mine_2.name: Mặc Nghiên Khoáng
prov_r6_30_mine_2.look: A small quarry of black slate on the mountainside, with split slabs stacked and rough inkstones lined up to dry.
prov_r6_30_mine_2.lore: Its slate makes the inkstones Thiên Xu's clerks grind their ink on. A stone from here is said to grind ink without a sound.

prov_r6_31_village_1.name: Hàn Mạch Thôn
prov_r6_31_village_1.look: Stone houses among small walled fields of pink-flowering buckwheat on a high forest edge.
prov_r6_31_village_1.lore: Its people grow buckwheat where wheat will not ripen and keep goats on the badland slopes. Their buckwheat noodles are sold as far as Thanh Bách.

prov_r6_31_beast_lair_2.name: Thạch Tích Đài
prov_r6_31_beast_lair_2.look: A red badland ledge where lizards the size of dogs lie unmoving in the sun, grey as the rock.
prov_r6_31_beast_lair_2.lore: Stone lizards bite and do not let go, and their skin turns arrows. Their shed skins are used to line armour.

prov_r6_32_peak_1.name: Hồng Nha Phong
prov_r6_32_peak_1.look: A lone red rock tooth standing out of the badlands.
prov_r6_32_peak_1.lore: Its qi runs to Earth. Travellers steer by it across the gullies.

prov_r6_32_mine_2.name: Thiên Thanh Khoáng
prov_r6_32_mine_2.look: Shallow pits in copper-stained mountain rock, with sky-blue turquoise chips glittering in the spoil.
prov_r6_32_mine_2.lore: Turquoise from here is carved into beads and inlays at Bích Khê. The crews keep the best chips in their cheeks until they are paid.

prov_r6_33_peak_1.name: Hợp Giác Phong
prov_r6_33_peak_1.look: Two sharp horns of grey rock rising from one mountain above the split-stone fields.
prov_r6_33_peak_1.lore: Its qi runs to Metal. Herders say the horns lean a little closer each century.

prov_r6_34_peak_1.name: Lộc Giác Phong
prov_r6_34_peak_1.look: A forested peak with branching rock ribs at its summit, like a stag's antlers.
prov_r6_34_peak_1.lore: Its qi runs to Wood. Hunters will not shoot within sight of it.

prov_r6_4_village_1.name: Hải Đê Thôn
prov_r6_4_village_1.look: Thatched houses on low ground behind a long grassy earth dike, with fishing boats drawn up on the seaward side.
prov_r6_4_village_1.lore: Its fields lie below the level of the sea, and the whole village mends the dike together each autumn. A child born in a storm is called a dike child and is first to carry earth.

prov_r6_4_forest_2.name: Phục Tùng Lâm
prov_r6_4_forest_2.look: Pines bent flat along the ground by the sea wind, their trunks crawling over the dunes.
prov_r6_4_forest_2.lore: The wind off the northern sea has laid these trees down. Hải Đê's people gather driftwood and pine cones here and nothing else.

prov_r6_5_town_1.name: Tạo Chu Trấn
prov_r6_5_town_1.look: A walled town on a sheltered bay with ship hulls on slipways along the shore and fir logs seasoning in great stacks.
prov_r6_5_town_1.lore: Its yards build fishing boats and coasters of fir for the northern coast and for Khai Dương's merchants. Every keel is laid facing the dawn, as in Khai Dương.

prov_r6_5_forest_2.name: Long Cốt Lâm
prov_r6_5_forest_2.look: Tall, straight hemlock firs on the flat behind the bay, with skid roads cut down to the water.
prov_r6_5_forest_2.lore: Its hard firs make the keels of Tạo Chu, and its name is the shipwrights' word for a keel. A tree is marked for a keel ten years before it is cut.

prov_r6_6_village_1.name: Mật Phong Thôn
prov_r6_6_village_1.look: A forest village whose walls are lined with hollow-log hives, the air humming all summer.
prov_r6_6_village_1.lore: Its people sell honey and wax as far as Thạch Kiều Thành. Bees that forage on the vein above the village make a darker honey that alchemists buy by weight.

prov_r6_6_spirit_vein_2.name: Thanh Đằng Mạch
prov_r6_6_spirit_vein_2.look: A hillside wrapped in green vines thick as arms, flowering out of season.
prov_r6_6_spirit_vein_2.lore: Its qi runs to Wood. The vines grow back overnight when cut, and the Mật Phong beekeepers set their hives at its edge.

prov_r6_7_village_1.name: Tích Thán Thôn
prov_r6_7_village_1.look: Smoky clay kilns among the trees, with sacks of charcoal piled by the lane and every face streaked black.
prov_r6_7_village_1.lore: Its people burn charcoal for the smiths of Khai Dương and Thanh Bách, cutting the forest in a twenty-year ring.

prov_r6_7_forest_2.name: Ngân Dương Lâm
prov_r6_7_forest_2.look: Pale-barked poplars on the hillsides, their leaves flashing silver in the wind.
prov_r6_7_forest_2.lore: Charcoal-burners let this wood grow back between cuttings. Its fast-growing poplar is the cheapest fuel in Dao Quang.

prov_r6_8_town_1.name: Cự Môn Trấn
prov_r6_8_town_1.look: A stone-walled harbour town between the forest and the cliffs, its gate set between two great boulders.
prov_r6_8_town_1.lore: Named for the Dipper's second star-lord, it ships timber and red iron and supplies the patrols bound for the high ranges. Its people took in the miners of Hắc Thạch Trấn after 874.

prov_r6_8_spirit_vein_2.name: Hải Vụ Mạch
prov_r6_8_spirit_vein_2.look: A forested hollow near the coast where sea fog gathers and lies all day, beading every leaf.
prov_r6_8_spirit_vein_2.lore: Its qi runs to Water. Fishermen of Cự Môn say the fog here never lifts until the tide turns.

prov_r6_8_ruin_3.name: Hắc Thạch Trấn
prov_r6_8_ruin_3.look: Empty stone houses of dark slate stepped up a bare mountain slope, their doors gone and their hearths cold.
prov_r6_8_ruin_3.lore: Phá Quân Môn's miners built this town in 760. When the rebel sect was destroyed in 874 the town passed to Cửu Cao Phái with the other holdings, but its people had already fled to Cự Môn, and none came back.

prov_r6_9_peak_1.name: Quan Triều Phong
prov_r6_9_peak_1.look: A steep grey peak over the sea cliffs, often capped with a single cloud.
prov_r6_9_peak_1.lore: Fishermen of Cự Môn read the weather by its cloud. Its qi runs to Water.
